“I'm going, Master Will—I really am,” the Black man answered at once. “I'm almost out at the end now.”

“Out at the end!” Legrand practically screamed. “Are you saying you're at the end of that branch?”

“Nearly at the end, master—o-o-o-oh! Lord have mercy! What's this up here on the tree?”

“Well!” cried Legrand, greatly excited. “What is it?”

“Why, it's just a skull. Somebody left their head up in the tree, and the crows have eaten every bit of flesh off it.”

“A skull, you say! Very good. How is it attached to the branch? What's holding it there?”

“Let me look, master. Well, this is a very strange thing, I swear. There's a great big nail through the skull, fastening it to the tree.”

“Now, Jupiter, do exactly what I tell you. Do you hear?”

“Yes, master.”

“Then listen carefully. Find the skull's left eye.”

“Ha! That's a good one! There aren't any eyes left at all.”

“Damn your stupidity! Can you tell your right hand from your left?”

“Yes, I know that. I know all about that. My left hand is the one I chop wood with.”

“Of course! You're left-handed, and your left eye is on the same side as your left hand. Now I suppose you can find the skull's left eye, or the hole where its left eye used to be. Have you found it?”

There was a long silence. At last Jupiter asked,

“Is the skull's left eye on the same side as its left hand too? Because this skull hasn't got any hands at all. Never mind! I've found the left eye now. Here's the left eye! What should I do with it?”

“Drop the beetle through it, as far as the string will let it go. But be careful to keep hold of the string.”

“That's done, Master Will. It's easy enough to put the bug through the hole. Watch out for it down there!”

Throughout this conversation we could see no part of Jupiter, but the beetle he had lowered now appeared at the end of the string. It shone like a ball of polished gold in the last rays of the setting sun, which still faintly lit the high ground where we stood. The beetle hung well clear of every branch and, if dropped, would have landed at our feet. Legrand immediately took the scythe and cleared a circle three or four yards across directly beneath the insect. When he had finished, he told Jupiter to release the string and climb down from the tree.

The witness could not be sure whether the voice belonged to a man or a woman. He could not understand the words, but thought the language was Spanish. His description of the room and the bodies matched the account we gave yesterday.

“Henri Duval, a neighbor who works as a silversmith, states that he was among the first people to enter the house. He generally supports Musèt's account. Once they forced their way inside, they shut the door again to keep out the crowd, which was gathering very quickly despite the late hour. This witness thinks the high-pitched voice belonged to an Italian. He was certain it was not French. He could not be sure that the speaker was a man; it might have been a woman. He did not know Italian and could not make out any words, but the sound of the voice convinced him the speaker was Italian. He knew Madame L. and her daughter and had often spoken with both. He was certain that the high-pitched voice belonged to neither of the dead women.

“——Odenheimer, restaurant owner. This witness came forward of his own accord. As he speaks no French, he was questioned through an interpreter. He comes from Amsterdam. He was passing the house when he heard the screams. They continued for several minutes, probably ten. They were long and loud, and extremely frightening and distressing. He was among those who entered the building. He agreed with all the earlier evidence except on one point. He was certain the high-pitched voice belonged to a man, a Frenchman. He could not understand the words. They were loud, rapid, and uneven, apparently spoken in fear as well as anger. The voice was harsh—more harsh than high-pitched. He would not describe it as high-pitched. The deep, rough voice repeatedly said ‘sacré’ and ‘diable,’ and once ‘mon Dieu.’

“Jules Mignaud, banker at Mignaud et Fils, Rue Deloraine. He is the older Mignaud. Madame L'Espanaye owned some property. She had opened an account with his bank in the spring eight years earlier. She often deposited small amounts. She had never withdrawn anything until three days before her death, when she came in herself and withdrew 4,000 francs. The bank paid her in gold, and a clerk accompanied the money home.

“Adolphe Le Bon, a clerk at Mignaud et Fils, states that around noon on that day he accompanied Madame L'Espanaye to her home, carrying the 4,000 francs in two bags. When the door opened, Mademoiselle L. appeared and took one bag from his hands, while the old lady took the other.

“I agree. It's the best thing to do. Should we just hold hands and swear that we—”

“Oh no, that won't do for this. That's good enough for little ordinary things—especially with girls, because they go back on you anyway and tell everything if they get mad—but something this big ought to be in writing. And blood.”

Tom welcomed the idea with his whole being. It was profound, dark, and terrible; the hour, the circumstances, and their surroundings all suited it. He picked up a clean pine shingle lying in the moonlight, took a small piece of red chalk from his pocket, and positioned his work where the moon would light it. Then he laboriously scrawled these lines, gripping his tongue between his teeth with every slow downward stroke and relaxing it on the upward strokes.

“Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swear they will keep quiet about This and They wish They may Drop down dead on the Spot if They ever Tell and Rot.”

Huckleberry was full of admiration for Tom's skill at writing and the grandeur of his language. He immediately took a pin from his lapel and prepared to prick himself, but Tom said:

“Wait! Don't do that. A pin's brass. It might have that green stuff on it.”

“What green stuff?”

“It's poison, that's what. Just swallow some sometime—you'll see.”

So Tom unwound the thread from one of his needles, and each boy pricked the pad of his thumb and squeezed out a drop of blood. Eventually, after a good deal of squeezing, Tom managed to sign his initials, using the tip of his little finger as a pen. Then he showed Huckleberry how to write an H and an F, and the oath was complete. They buried the shingle near the wall with some gloomy ceremonies and chants, and considered the chains binding their tongues locked, with the key thrown away.

A figure now crept quietly through a gap at the other end of the ruined building, but they failed to notice it.

“Tom,” Huckleberry whispered, “does this mean we can never tell—for as long as we live?”

“Of course it does. Whatever happens, we've got to keep quiet. We'd drop down dead—don't you know that?”

“Yes, I guess that's right.”

They went on whispering for a little while. Then a dog began a long, mournful howl just outside, less than ten feet away. The boys suddenly clutched each other in an agony of terror.

“Which one of us does he mean?” Huckleberry gasped.

“I don't know—look through the crack. Quick!”

“No, you do it, Tom!”

“I can't—I can't do it, Huck!”
